text: Every document SO-48217 has generated - the invoice, the credit memo, the cash receipt - has an accounting consequence. None of it was typed in by hand. Let's look at what those entries actually are.

Receivables doesn't just store an amount; each transaction type ties to a defined accounting event. Subledger Accounting holds rules that say, for a given event, which accounts get debited and credited, and how. You covered this concept on its own already - now you're seeing it fire for a real sequence of events.

Three entries came out of this cycle. The invoice: debit Receivable, credit Revenue, fifty-five thousand, one hundred dollars. The credit memo: debit Revenue, credit Receivable, two thousand, seven hundred fifty-five dollars, reversing part of that. The cash receipt: debit Cash, credit Receivable, fifty-two thousand, three hundred forty-five dollars - it never touches revenue again.

Add up the receivable side: fifty-five thousand, one hundred, minus two thousand, seven hundred fifty-five, minus fifty-two thousand, three hundred forty-five. That's zero. The receivable for this invoice is fully cleared - exactly matching what you already saw happen in Receivables.

Troubleshooting unexpected accounting here really means troubleshooting the SLA rule that fired, not hunting for a manual typo - because there usually isn't one. Up next, lesson twenty-one: how these entries actually get from Subledger Accounting into the General Ledger.
